You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

4. After the verdict, save the program that reproduced all the pairs to the task's file, replacing any older version, then finish.

# Continual ARC

Use this procedure for task-id grid puzzles with an available program library.

1. For every reply in an instance, output only one supported action as a JSON object on the last line; omit commentary. Check `programs/<task id>.py`; if present, run `transform(grid)` on the test input and submit that exact output before requesting demos. After a wrong verdict, do not retry the same output; use the demo-and-repair loop below.
2. Infer the transformation jointly from all demos. Request a demo only if its possible outcomes distinguish plausible rules; weigh its cost against remaining attempts and demo allowance.
3. Implement or repair a candidate, then execute it on the test and every received input-output pair. Require exact shape and cell-by-cell agreement with all pairs before submission; submit only the checked program output, not a manually guessed grid. Keep the prior library file intact until a candidate passes every demo; if none does, leave the library file unchanged. After a wrong verdict, treat it only as evidence the current rule is wrong—not as localization or confirmation of any particular cells—and revisit the demonstrations before changing the rule.
4. Once the transformation is supported by every demo, prefer another discriminating demo over speculative submissions when uncertainty remains. Do not claim verification if demo agreement is incomplete.
5. After a correct verdict, save the verified transform at `programs/<task id>.py`, replacing any older version, then finish.

Validate parsing and panel geometry explicitly: locate the divider and identify panel bounds/orientation from the input; do not infer layout from color counts alone. Derive each panel's background/foreground from evidence and check whether output represents an overlay, comparison, or another relation against every full demo before encoding it. Avoid hardcoded colors or guessed majority rules unless demos establish them.

Each instance has its own attempt and demo costs. Feedback on a submission is only correct/incorrect, so use it to trigger hypothesis revision, not as a cell-level diagnosis.
